ETA in 5, PNV in 14, CCOO in 18, PCE(m-l) in 19. Islamic slots anchored in Spanish Sahara (Djemaa in 10, Bassiri's movement in 12) and Arab student milieus. CNT and Tierno Galván's PSI not placed.

0.name: Comunión Tradicionalista
0.text:
The Traditionalist Communion is the organisation of Carlism, the legitimist movement that fought three civil wars for its own line of kings and supplied the Requeté militias to the 1936 uprising. Its claimant is Prince Javier de Borbón-Parma, whose son Carlos Hugo was expelled from Spain in December 1968; Franco's choice of Juan Carlos de Borbón as successor in July 1969 has pushed the movement into open opposition.

Rooted in Navarre and drawing tens of thousands to the yearly Montejurra rally, Carlism defends the Catholic faith, the historic fueros of the regions and a monarchy limited by tradition rather than parliament. Under Carlos Hugo its younger activists are turning towards federalism and workers' self-management, alarming the old traditionalists. Its leverage lies in Navarrese loyalty and its claim to the throne.

5.name: Euskadi Ta Askatasuna
5.text:
Euskadi Ta Askatasuna, Basque Homeland and Freedom, was founded in 1959 by young nationalists frustrated with the passivity of the Basque Nationalist Party. In June 1968 it killed its first victim, a Civil Guard, and two months later the San Sebastián police chief Melitón Manzanas; the state of exception and mass arrests that followed have decimated it, and sixteen of its members await court-martial in Burgos.

ETA combines Basque independence with revolutionary socialism, casting its struggle as national and social liberation in the mould of Algeria, Cuba and Vietnam. Its strategy of action, repression and further action aims to provoke a popular uprising. Its base is young, Basque-speaking and drawn from seminaries, factories and villages, and the coming trial is turning its prisoners into national martyrs.

6.name: Círculos Doctrinales José Antonio
6.text:
The José Antonio Doctrinal Circles were founded in 1959 by veteran 'old shirt' Falangists led by Luis González Vicén, who accuse Franco of betraying the national-syndicalist revolution of José Antonio Primo de Rivera. Tolerated on the margins of the Movement, they run clubs, lectures and bulletins in Madrid and the provinces and attract disillusioned young Falangists.

The Circles reject the regime's alliance with big capital, the Church hierarchy and the monarchy, and they denounce the Opus Dei technocrats, the American bases and the opening to foreign capital as a sell-out of Spanish sovereignty. They call for a syndicalist economy, land reform and a truly independent foreign policy. Their leverage is small but moral: they speak for the Falangist rank and file who feel their revolution was stolen.

7.name: Brigada Político-Social
7.text:
The Political-Social Brigade is the political police of the General Directorate of Security, charged since the Civil War with hunting communists, anarchists, separatists and every other enemy of the regime. Its most feared officers include Roberto Conesa in Madrid and the brothers Antonio and Vicente Juan Creix in Barcelona, whose interrogation rooms at the Puerta del Sol and the Vía Layetana are notorious for torture.

The Brigade knows no ideology beyond the defence of Franco's order, and it used the state of exception of early 1969 to round up students and labour activists by the hundred. It works alongside military intelligence and the Civil Guard. Its leverage lies in its files, its informers in factories and universities and the impunity granted by the military courts and the Public Order Tribunal.

8.name: Círculo Amilí de Madrid
8.text:
The Amili Circle of Madrid is a small group of Lebanese Shia students, most of them from Jabal Amil in southern Lebanon, who have come to study medicine and engineering in Madrid under Spain's cultural agreements with the Arab world. They meet in each other's rooms for prayers and the mourning of Ashura, and keep in touch with home through letters and visiting relatives.

They admire Imam Musa al-Sadr, elected in 1969 to head Lebanon's new Supreme Islamic Shia Council, and share his programme of a modern, socially engaged Shia Islam that lifts the poor of the south without revolution. They keep entirely out of Spanish politics. Their weight is negligible, but they form a bridge between Spain and the awakening Shia community of Lebanon.

9.name: Círculo de Nayaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle gathers a handful of Iraqi Shia students in Madrid and Granada, some of whom left Iraq after the Ba'athist crackdown on the Najaf seminaries in 1969. They look to Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim and the young theorist Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr, and pass around the lectures of the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who teaches in Najaf.

The circle holds that Muslims must be ruled under the guidance of the senior clergy and condemns both the secular Ba'ath and Western influence. Its members are devout, secretive and few, keeping clear of the Spanish police while collecting funds for persecuted clerics in Iraq. Their importance lies only in their links to the clerical networks now challenging the Ba'ath in Baghdad and the Shah in Tehran.

10.name: Asamblea General del Sáhara
10.text:
The Djemaa, the General Assembly of the Sahara, was created by the Spanish authorities in May 1967 to give the tribes of Spanish Sahara a representative body of chiefs and notables under colonial tutelage. Its president is the elderly notable Jatri Uld Said Uld Yumani, and it meets in El Aaiún under the eye of the Governor-General.

The Djemaa embodies the traditional order of the desert: Maliki Sunni Islam, tribal hierarchy, the authority of elders and loyalty to Spain as protector against Moroccan and Mauritanian claims. It approves Spanish administration and asks in return for development, schools, wells and pastures. Its leverage lies in the chiefs' hold over their kinsmen and in Madrid's need for Sahrawi partners as the Bu Craa phosphate deposits are developed.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, who leads it from exile in Beirut. Banned throughout the Arab world, it works in secret cells in Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon, and among the Jordanian and Palestinian students who have come in growing numbers to study medicine at Spanish universities.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and socialism as alien to Islam and works to restore the Caliphate by winning over army officers and intellectuals. Its members study al-Nabhani's writings in disciplined circles and argue with fellow students drawn to Fatah and the Marxist fronts. In Spain it has no public face, but it offers a militant few a total alternative to both blocs.

12.name: Harakat Tahrir Saqiya al-Hamra wa Wadi al-Dhahab
12.english: Movement for the Liberation of Saguia el-Hamra and Wadi el-Dhahab
12.native_full: Harakat Tahrir Saqiya al-Hamra wa Wadi al-Dhahab
12.text:
The Movement for the Liberation of Saguia el-Hamra and Wadi el-Dhahab is a clandestine organisation founded in 1969 by Muhammad Sidi Ibrahim Bassiri, a young Sahrawi teacher educated in Morocco, Cairo and Damascus, who runs a Koranic school in Smara. It recruits quietly among the townspeople of El Aaiún and Smara, Sahrawis serving in the Spanish forces and workers in the new phosphate industry.

The movement blends Islamic reformism with modern nationalism: it calls for education, the renewal of Muslim life and social progress, and for gradual autonomy leading to independence from Spain, rejecting both Moroccan annexation and armed struggle. Its leverage lies in its appeal to a new, urbanised generation of Sahrawis and in Bassiri's moral authority as a scholar.

13.name: Los tecnócratas
13.text:
The Technocrats are the Catholic economists, lawyers and engineers, many of them members of Opus Dei, who have dominated Franco's government since the 'monochrome' cabinet of October 1969. Their patron is Admiral Luis Carrero Blanco, the Vice-President, and their strategist Laureano López Rodó, Commissioner of the Development Plan, while Gregorio López Bravo runs foreign affairs.

They believe economic growth, planning and integration into the European market will make Spain prosperous and political reform unnecessary, while securing the monarchy of Juan Carlos as the continuation of the regime. Apolitical in style but ruthless in practice, they emerged victorious from the MATESA scandal their Falangist rivals used against them. Their leverage lies in Carrero's confidence, the economic ministries and the businesses thriving on the boom.

14.name: Euzko Alderdi Jeltzalea – Partido Nacionalista Vasco
14.native_full: Euzko Alderdi Jeltzalea – Partido Nacionalista Vasco
14.text:
The Basque Nationalist Party, founded by Sabino Arana in 1895, is the historic party of Basque nationalism. Banned since 1937, it sustains the Basque Government in exile in Paris under lehendakari Jesús María de Leizaola, while its clandestine organisation inside the country is led by Juan de Ajuriaguerra.

The party is Christian democratic, Catholic and moderate, seeking self-government for the Basque Country within a democratic order and rejecting violence, a stance that has cost it many young militants to ETA. It is firmly pro-Western and a member of the European Christian democratic family. Its base lies among the Basque middle classes, the clergy and the Basque-speaking countryside, and its leverage rests on historic legitimacy and international contacts.

15.name: Los Siete Grandes
15.text:
The Big Seven are Spain's great private banks – Español de Crédito, Central, Hispano Americano, Bilbao, Vizcaya, Santander and Popular – which together hold most of the nation's deposits and, through their industrial portfolios, control much of its heavy industry, electricity, shipbuilding and construction. Among their chiefs are Emilio Botín of the Banco de Santander and the Opus Dei numerary Luis Valls-Taberner of the Banco Popular.

The banks thrive on the protection, cheap credit and closed market of the Francoist economy and on the growth of the Spanish miracle. They want order, labour peace and gradual integration into Europe, and they fear both communism and genuine competition. Their leverage lies in interlocking directorships, privileged access to ministers and the dependence of entire industries on their credit.

16.name: Círculo de Economía
16.text:
The Circle of Economy was founded in Barcelona in 1958 by young Catalan businessmen, managers and economists convinced that the stagnant, autarkic Francoist economy had to open up. Among its prominent members is the industrialist Carles Ferrer Salat, and it has become a forum where entrepreneurs, academics and even discreet opposition figures debate Spain's future.

The Circle stands for a market economy, competition, entry into the European Economic Community and modern business and labour relations, which it believes demand gradual political liberalisation as well. It criticises state monopolies, the National Industry Institute and the vertical syndicate. Its leverage lies in the weight of Catalan industry, its links to the banks and its influence on the economic thinking of a new generation.

17.name: Asociación para la Defensa de la Naturaleza
17.english: Association for the Defence of Nature
17.native_full: Asociación para la Defensa de la Naturaleza
17.text:
The Association for the Defence of Nature was founded in 1968 as the Spanish branch of the World Wildlife Fund by the naturalist and broadcaster Félix Rodríguez de la Fuente, the biologist José Antonio Valverde and other scientists and patrons. Valverde's long campaign to save the Guadalquivir marshes was crowned by the creation of the Doñana National Park in 1969.

ADENA campaigns to protect endangered species such as the Iberian lynx, the imperial eagle and the wolf, for new reserves and against the drainage of wetlands and the destruction of the coast by tourism. Strictly apolitical, it enjoys prominent patrons in the establishment. Its leverage lies in Rodríguez de la Fuente's enormous popularity on television and radio and in a new middle-class awareness of nature.

18.name: Comisiones Obreras
18.text:
The Workers' Commissions grew out of the strike committees of the Asturian mines and the industrial belts of Madrid, Barcelona and Biscay in the early 1960s and became a permanent clandestine union movement that works inside the official vertical syndicate. Declared illegal by the Supreme Court in 1967, its leaders face constant arrest; Marcelino Camacho, its best-known figure, has been in prison since 1967.

The Commissions fight for higher wages, free trade unions, the right to strike and democratic freedoms. Communists of the PCE are the strongest force within them, but Catholic worker activists from the HOAC and JOC, socialists and independents also play leading roles. Their leverage lies in the factories: strikes in metalworking, mining and construction are now the regime's most persistent challenge.

19.name: Partido Comunista de España (marxista-leninista)
19.text:
The Communist Party of Spain (Marxist-Leninist) was founded in 1964 by militants who broke with Santiago Carrillo's PCE, accusing it of Soviet revisionism and of seeking peaceful coexistence with Francoism. Led from exile by Elena Ódena and Raúl Marco, it looks to Beijing and Tirana for inspiration and support, and its cells operate among students and young workers.

The party calls for a revolutionary people's war to overthrow Franco and the 'Yankee imperialists' who prop him up through the bases, and for a federal people's republic. It denounces both Moscow's 'social-imperialism' and the PCE's policy of national reconciliation. Small, sectarian and relentlessly pursued by the police, it compensates for its weakness with uncompromising militancy.

20.name: Fuerza Nueva
20.text:
Fuerza Nueva is the publishing house and political association founded in 1966 by the Madrid notary Blas Piñar, former director of the Institute of Hispanic Culture and a member of the regime's councils. Its weekly magazine and lecture tours rally Francoist loyalists who fear that the regime is losing its soul to the technocrats and to the Church's new progressives.

Fuerza Nueva preaches National Catholicism, unconditional loyalty to Franco and the 'spirit of 18 July', and defends the victors of the Civil War against any liberalisation, regional autonomy or dialogue with the opposition. Its audience is drawn from war veterans, the provincial middle classes, traditional Catholics and young street activists. Its leverage lies in Piñar's oratory and its role as the conscience of the regime's hard core.
